# assert_cmd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/assert_cmd/^2/

## Expand description

**Assert ** - Easy command initialization and assertions.

`Command``assert_cmd` aims to simplify the process for doing integration testing of CLIs, including:

- Finding your crate’s binary to test
- Assert on the result of your program’s run.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

Create a [ Command](https://docs.rs/cmd/struct.Command.html):

- `Command::new(path)`
- `Command::from_std(...)`
- `Command::cargo_bin(name)`

Configure a [ Command](https://docs.rs/cmd/struct.Command.html):

- `arg`/- `args`
- `current_dir`
- `env`/- `envs`/- `env_remove`/- `env_clear`
- `write_stdin`/- `pipe_stdin`
- `timeout`

Validate a [ Command](https://docs.rs/cmd/struct.Command.html):

- `ok`/- `unwrap`/- `unwrap_err`
- `assert`

Note: [ Command](https://docs.rs/cmd/struct.Command.html) is provided as a convenience. Extension traits for

[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/struct.Command.html)

`std::process::Command``Output` are provided for interoperability:[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Here’s a trivial example:

```
use assert_cmd::Command;
let mut cmd = Command::cargo_bin("bin_fixture").unwrap();
cmd.assert().success();
```
And a little of everything:

```
use assert_cmd::Command;
let mut cmd = Command::cargo_bin("bin_fixture").unwrap();
let assert = cmd
    .arg("-A")
    .env("stdout", "hello")
    .env("exit", "42")
    .write_stdin("42")
    .assert();
assert
    .failure()
    .code(42)
    .stdout("hello\n");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#relevant-crates)Relevant crates

Other crates that might be useful in testing command line programs.

- [escargot](https://crates.io/crates/escargot)for more control over configuring the crate’s binary.
- [duct](https://crates.io/crates/duct)for orchestrating multiple processes.- or [commandspec](https://crates.io/crates/commandspec)for easier writing of commands

- or
- [rexpect](https://crates.io/crates/rexpect)for testing interactive programs.
- [assert_fs](https://crates.io/crates/assert_fs)for filesystem fixtures and assertions.- or [tempfile](https://crates.io/crates/tempfile)for scratchpad directories.

- or
- [dir-diff](https://crates.io/crates/dir-diff)for testing file side-effects.

[§](https://docs.rs#migrating-from-assert_cli-v06)Migrating from `assert_cli` v0.6

`assert_cmd` is the successor to [the original  assert_cli](https://crates.io/crates/assert_cli/0.6.3):

- More flexible, reusable assertions (also used by [assert_fs](https://crates.io/crates/assert_fs)).
- Can integrate with other process-management crates, like `duct`.
- Addresses several architectural problems.

Key points in migrating from `assert_cli`:

- The command-under-test is run eagerly, with assertions happening immediately.
- `success()`
- `stdout`/- `stderr`aren’t automatically trimmed before being passed to the- `Predicate`.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::cmd::`- [Command](https://docs.rs/cmd/struct.Command.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [assert](https://docs.rs/assert/index.html)
- `std::process::Output`
- [cargo](https://docs.rs/cargo/index.html)
- Simplify running `bin`s in a Cargo project.
- [cmd](https://docs.rs/cmd/index.html)
- `std::process::Command`

- Simplify one-off runs of programs.

- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_name.html)- name - Deprecated
- Deprecated, replaced with `pkg_name`
- [pkg_](https://docs.rs/macro.pkg_name.html)- name
- Allows you to pull the name from your Cargo.toml at compile time.

# criterion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/criterion/^0.8/

## Expand description

A statistics-driven micro-benchmarking library written in Rust.

This crate is a microbenchmarking library which aims to provide strong statistical confidence in detecting and estimating the size of performance improvements and regressions, while also being easy to use.

See
[the user guide](https://criterion-rs.github.io/book/index.html)
for examples as well as details on the measurement and analysis process,
and the output.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features:

- Collects detailed statistics, providing strong confidence that changes to performance are real, not measurement noise.
- Produces detailed charts, providing thorough understanding of your code’s performance behavior.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [async_](https://docs.rs/async_executor/index.html)- executor
- This module defines a trait that can be used to plug in different Futures executors into Criterion.rs’ async benchmarking support.
- [measurement](https://docs.rs/measurement/index.html)
- This module defines a set of traits that can be used to plug different measurements (eg.
Unix’s Processor Time, CPU or GPU performance counters, etc.) into Criterion.rs. It also
includes the `WallTime`
- [profiler](https://docs.rs/profiler/index.html)
- This module provides an extension trait which allows in-process profilers
to be hooked into the `--profile-time`argument at compile-time. Users of out-of-process profilers such as perf don’t need to do anything special.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [criterion_](https://docs.rs/macro.criterion_group.html)- group
- Macro used to define a function group for the benchmark harness; see the
`criterion_main!`
- [criterion_](https://docs.rs/macro.criterion_main.html)- main
- Macro which expands to a benchmark harness.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncBencher.html)- Bencher
- Async/await variant of `Bencher`
- [Bencher](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html)
- Timer struct used to iterate a benchmarked function and measure the runtime.
- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/struct.BenchmarkGroup.html)- Group
- Structure used to group together a set of related benchmarks, along with custom configuration settings for groups of benchmarks. All benchmarks performed using a benchmark group will be grouped together in the final report.
- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/struct.BenchmarkId.html)- Id
- Simple structure representing an ID for a benchmark. The ID must be unique within a benchmark group.
- [Criterion](https://docs.rs/struct.Criterion.html)
- The benchmark manager
- [Plot](https://docs.rs/struct.PlotConfiguration.html)- Configuration
- Contains the configuration options for the plots generated by a particular benchmark or benchmark group.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Axis](https://docs.rs/enum.AxisScale.html)- Scale
- Axis scaling type. Specified via `PlotConfiguration::summary_scale`
- [Baseline](https://docs.rs/enum.Baseline.html)
- Baseline describes how the `baseline_directory`is handled.
- [Batch](https://docs.rs/enum.BatchSize.html)- Size
- Argument to `Bencher::iter_batched``Bencher::iter_batched_ref`
- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/enum.BenchmarkFilter.html)- Filter
- Benchmark filtering support.
- [Plotting](https://docs.rs/enum.PlottingBackend.html)- Backend
- Enum used to select the plotting backend.
- [Sampling](https://docs.rs/enum.SamplingMode.html)- Mode
- This enum allows the user to control how Criterion.rs chooses the iteration count when sampling.
The default is `Auto`, which will choose a method automatically based on the iteration time during the warm-up phase.
- [Throughput](https://docs.rs/enum.Throughput.html)
- Enum representing different ways of measuring the throughput of benchmarked code. If the throughput setting is configured for a benchmark then the estimated throughput will be reported as well as the time per iteration.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [black_](https://docs.rs/fn.black_box.html)- box - Deprecated
- A function that is opaque to the optimizer, used to prevent the compiler from optimizing away computations in a benchmark.

# insta - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/insta/^1/

## Expand description

**insta: a snapshot testing library for Rust**

[§](https://docs.rs#what-are-snapshot-tests)What are snapshot tests

Snapshots tests (also sometimes called approval tests) are tests that
assert values against a reference value (the snapshot).  This is similar
to how [ assert_eq!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.assert_eq.html) lets you compare a value against a reference value but
unlike simple string assertions, snapshot tests let you test against complex
values and come with comprehensive tools to review changes.

Snapshot tests are particularly useful if your reference values are very large or change often.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-it-looks-like)What it looks like:

```
#[test]
fn test_hello_world() {
    insta::assert_debug_snapshot!(vec![1, 2, 3]);
}
```
Where are the snapshots stored?  Right next to your test in a folder
called `snapshots` as individual [ .snap files](https://insta.rs/docs/snapshot-files/).

Got curious?

- [Read the introduction](https://insta.rs/docs/quickstart/)
- [Read the main documentation](https://insta.rs/docs/)which does not just cover the API of the crate but also many of the details of how it works.
- There is a screencast that shows the entire workflow: [watch the insta introduction screencast](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rCHrMqE4JOY&feature=youtu.be).

[§](https://docs.rs#writing-tests)Writing Tests

```
use insta::assert_debug_snapshot;
#[test]
fn test_snapshots() {
    assert_debug_snapshot!(vec![1, 2, 3]);
}
```
The recommended flow is to run the tests once, have them fail and check
if the result is okay.
By default, the new snapshots are stored next
to the old ones with the extra `.new` extension.  Once you are satisfied
move the new files over.  To simplify this workflow you can use
`cargo insta review` (requires
[ cargo-insta](https://crates.io/crates/cargo-insta)) which will let you
interactively review them:

```
$ cargo test
$ cargo insta review
```
[§](https://docs.rs#use-without-cargo-insta)Use Without `cargo-insta`

Note that `cargo-insta` is entirely optional.  You can also just use insta
directly from `cargo test` and control it via the `INSTA_UPDATE` environment
variable — see [Updating snapshots](https://docs.rs#updating-snapshots) for details.

You can for instance first run the tests and not write any new snapshots, and if you like them run the tests again and update them:

```
INSTA_UPDATE=no cargo test
INSTA_UPDATE=always cargo test
```
[§](https://docs.rs#assertion-macros)Assertion Macros

This crate exports multiple macros for snapshot testing:

- `assert_snapshot!`- `Display`
- `assert_debug_snapshot!`- `Debug`

The following macros require the use of [ serde::Serialize](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html):

- `assert_csv_snapshot!`- `csv`feature)
- `assert_toml_snapshot!`- `toml`feature)
- `assert_yaml_snapshot!`- `yaml`feature)
- `assert_ron_snapshot!`- `ron`feature)
- `assert_json_snapshot!`- `json`feature)
- `assert_compact_json_snapshot!`- `json`feature)

For macros that work with [ serde](https://docs.rs/serde/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde/index.html) this crate also permits redacting of
partial values.  See

[redactions in the documentation](https://insta.rs/docs/redactions/)for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#updating-snapshots)Updating snapshots

During test runs snapshots will be updated according to the `INSTA_UPDATE`
environment variable.  The default is `auto` which will write snapshots for
any failing tests into `.snap.new` files (if no CI is detected) so that
[ cargo-insta](https://crates.io/crates/cargo-insta) can pick them up for
review. Normally you don’t have to change this variable.

`INSTA_UPDATE` modes:

- `auto`: the default.- `no`for CI environments or- `new`otherwise
- `new`: writes snapshots for any failing tests into- `.snap.new`files, pending review
- `always`: writes snapshots for any failing tests into- `.snap`files, bypassing review
- `unseen`:- `always`for previously unseen snapshots or- `new`for existing snapshots
- `no`: does not write to snapshot files at all; just runs tests
- `force`: forcibly updates snapshot files, even if assertions pass

When `new`, `auto` or `unseen` is used, the
[ cargo-insta](https://crates.io/crates/cargo-insta) command can be used to
review the snapshots conveniently:

`$ cargo insta review`“enter” or “a” accepts a new snapshot, “escape” or “r” rejects, “space” or “s” skips the snapshot for now.

For more information [read the cargo insta
docs](https://insta.rs/docs/cli/).

[§](https://docs.rs#inline-snapshots)Inline Snapshots

Additionally snapshots can also be stored inline.  In that case the format
for the snapshot macros is `assert_snapshot!(reference_value, @"snapshot")`.
The leading at sign (`@`) indicates that the following string is the
reference value.  On review, `cargo-insta` will update the string with the
new value.

Example:

`assert_snapshot!(2 + 2, @"");`Like with normal snapshots, an initial test failure will write the proposed
value into a draft file (note that inline snapshots use `.pending-snap`
files rather than `.snap.new` files). Running `cargo insta review` will
review the proposed changes and update the source files on acceptance
automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

The following features exist:

- `csv`: enables CSV support (via- `serde`
- `json`: enables JSON support (via- `serde`
- `ron`: enables RON support (via- `serde`
- `toml`: enables TOML support (via- `serde`
- `yaml`: enables YAML support (via- `serde`
- `redactions`: enables support for redactions
- `filters`: enables support for filters
- `glob`: enables support for globbing (- `glob!`
- `colors`: enables color output (enabled by default)

For legacy reasons the `json` and `yaml` features are enabled by default in
limited capacity.  You will receive a deprecation warning if you are not
opting into them but for now the macros will continue to function.

Enabling any of the [ serde](https://docs.rs/serde/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde/index.html) based formats enables the hidden

`serde` feature
which gates some [specific APIs such as](https://docs.rs/serde/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde/index.html)

`serde`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Settings.html#method.set_info)

`Settings::set_info`[§](https://docs.rs#dependencies)Dependencies

[ insta](https://docs.rs/insta) tries to be light in dependencies but this is tricky to accomplish
given what it tries to do.
By default, it currently depends on

[for the](https://docs.rs/serde/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde/index.html)

`serde`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_toml_snapshot.html)

`assert_toml_snapshot!`[macros. In the future this default dependencies will be removed. To already benefit from this optimization you can disable the default features and manually opt into what you want.](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_yaml_snapshot.html)

`assert_yaml_snapshot!`[§](https://docs.rs#settings-1)Settings

There are some settings that can be changed on a per-thread (and thus
per-test) basis.  For more information see [Settings](https://docs.rs/struct.Settings.html).

Additionally, Insta will load a YAML config file with settings that change
the behavior of insta between runs.  It’s loaded from any of the following
locations: `.config/insta.yaml`, `insta.yaml` and `.insta.yaml` from the
workspace root.  The following config options exist:

```
behavior:
  # also set by INSTA_REQUIRE_FULL_MATCH
  require_full_match: true/false
  # also set by INSTA_FORCE_PASS
  force_pass: true/false
  # also set by INSTA_OUTPUT
  output: "diff" | "summary" | "minimal" | "none"
  # also set by INSTA_UPDATE
  update: "auto" | "new" | "always" | "no" | "unseen" | "force"
  # also set by INSTA_GLOB_FAIL_FAST
  glob_fail_fast: true/false
# these are used by cargo insta test
test:
  # also set by INSTA_TEST_RUNNER
  # cargo-nextest binary path can be explicitly set by INSTA_CARGO_NEXTEST_BIN
  runner: "auto" | "cargo-test" | "nextest"
  # whether to fallback to `cargo-test` if `nextest` is not available,
  # also set by INSTA_TEST_RUNNER_FALLBACK, default false
  runner_fallback: true/false
  # disable running doctests separately when using nextest
  disable_nextest_doctest: true/false
  # automatically assume --review was passed to cargo insta test
  auto_review: true/false
  # automatically assume --accept-unseen was passed to cargo insta test
  auto_accept_unseen: true/false
# these are used by cargo insta review
review:
  # also look for snapshots in ignored folders
  include_ignored: true / false
  # also look for snapshots in hidden folders
  include_hidden: true / false
  # show a warning if undiscovered (ignored or hidden) snapshots are found.
  # defaults to true but creates a performance hit.
  warn_undiscovered: true / false
```
[§](https://docs.rs#external-diff-tools)External Diff Tools

By default, insta displays diffs inline in unified format. You can configure
an external diff tool via the `INSTA_DIFF_TOOL` environment variable. When set,
insta writes the old and new snapshot contents to temporary files and invokes
your diff tool with those files as arguments.

```
# Use delta for syntax-highlighted diffs
export INSTA_DIFF_TOOL=delta
# With arguments
export INSTA_DIFF_TOOL="delta --side-by-side"
# Or any other diff tool
export INSTA_DIFF_TOOL=difftastic
```
This is a user-level setting (not project-level) since diff tool preference
varies by developer. The tool is invoked as `<tool> [args...] <old_file> <new_file>`.
If the tool fails to run, insta falls back to the built-in diff.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-faster-runs)Optional: Faster Runs

Insta benefits from being compiled in release mode, even as dev dependency.
It will compile slightly slower once, but use less memory, have faster diffs
and just generally be more fun to use.  To achieve that, opt [ insta](https://docs.rs/insta) and

[(the diffing library) into higher optimization in your](https://docs.rs/similar/2.7.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/similar/index.html)

`similar``Cargo.toml`:```
[profile.dev.package.insta]
opt-level = 3
[profile.dev.package.similar]
opt-level = 3
```
You can also disable the default features of [ insta](https://docs.rs/insta) which will cut down on
the compile time a bit by removing some quality of life features.

# predicates - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/predicates/^3/

## Expand description

Composable first-order predicate functions.

This library implements an interface to “predicates” - boolean-valued functions of one argument. This allows combinatorial logic to be created and assembled at runtime and then used one or more times for evaluating values. This sort of object is really useful when creating filters and checks that can be changed at runtime with user interaction - it allows a clean separation of concerns where the configuration code can be used to build up a predicate, and then that predicate can be given to the code that does the actual filtering without the filtering code knowing anything about user configuration. See the examples for how this can work.

[§](https://docs.rs#installation)Installation

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
predicates = "3.1.4"
```
A [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html) is available to bring in all extension traits as well as providing
`prelude::predicate` which focuses on the 90% case of the API.

`use predicates::prelude::*;`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

The simplest predicates are [ predicate::always](https://docs.rs/constant/fn.always.html) and

[, which always returns](https://docs.rs/constant/fn.never.html)

`predicate::never``true` and always returns `false`, respectively. The values are simply ignored when
evaluating against these predicates:```
use predicates::prelude::*;
let always_true = predicate::always();
assert_eq!(true, always_true.eval(&5));
let always_false = predicate::never();
assert_eq!(false, always_false.eval(&5));
```
Pre-made predicates are available for types that implement the `PartialOrd` and
`PartialEq` traits. The following example uses `lt`, but `eq`, `ne`, `le`, `gt`,
`ge` are also available.

```
use predicates::prelude::*;
let less_than_ten = predicate::lt(10);
assert_eq!(true, less_than_ten.eval(&9));
assert_eq!(false, less_than_ten.eval(&11));
```
Any function over a reference to the desired `Item` that returns `bool`
can easily be made into a `Predicate` using the [ predicate::function](https://docs.rs/function/fn.function.html)
function.

```
use predicates::prelude::*;
let bound = 5;
let predicate_fn = predicate::function(|&x| x >= bound);
let between_5_and_10 = predicate_fn.and(predicate::le(10));
assert_eq!(true, between_5_and_10.eval(&7));
assert_eq!(false, between_5_and_10.eval(&3));
```
The `Predicate` type is actually a trait, and that trait implements a
number of useful combinator functions. For example, evaluating for a value
between two other values can be accomplished as follows:

```
use predicates::prelude::*;
let between_5_and_10 = predicate::ge(5).and(predicate::le(10));
assert_eq!(true, between_5_and_10.eval(&7));
assert_eq!(false, between_5_and_10.eval(&11));
assert_eq!(false, between_5_and_10.eval(&4));
```
The `Predicate` trait is pretty simple, the core of it is an
implementation of a `eval` function that takes a single argument and
returns a `bool`. Implementing a custom `Predicate` still allows all the
usual combinators of the `Predicate` trait to work!

```
use std::fmt;
use predicates::prelude::*;
struct IsTheAnswer;
impl Predicate<i32> for IsTheAnswer {
    fn eval(&self, variable: &i32) -> bool {
        *variable == 42
    }
}
impl predicates::reflection::PredicateReflection for IsTheAnswer {}
impl fmt::Display for IsTheAnswer {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "var.is_the_answer()")
    }
}
assert_eq!(true, IsTheAnswer.eval(&42));
let almost_the_answer = IsTheAnswer.or(predicate::in_iter(vec![41, 43]));
assert_eq!(true, almost_the_answer.eval(&41));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#choosing-a-predicate)Choosing a Predicate

General predicates

- `predicate::always`
- `predicate::never`
- `predicate::function`
- `predicate::in_iter`- `Iterator`.- `predicate::in_iter(...).sort`
- `predicate::in_hash`

- `predicate::eq`- `predicate::float::is_close`- `eq`for floating point values.

- `predicate::ne`
- `predicate::ge`
- `predicate::gt`
- `predicate::le`
- `predicate::lt`
- `predicate::name`

Combinators

- `pred_a.and(pred_b)`
- `pred_a.or(pred_b)`
- `pred_a.not()`

`String` predicates

- `predicate::str::is_empty`
- `str_pred = predicate::path::eq_file(...).utf8`
- `predicate::str::diff`- `eq`except report a diff. See- `DifferencePredicate`
- `predicate::str::starts_with`
- `predicate::str::ends_with`
- `predicate::str::contains`- `predicate::str::contains(...).count`

- `predicate::str::is_match`- `predicate::str::is_match(...).count`

- `str_pred.trim`- `str_pred`.
- `str_pred.normalize`- `str_pred`.
- `bytes_pred = str_pred.from_utf8()`

File system predicates

- `predicate::path::exists`
- `predicate::path::missing`
- `predicate::path::is_dir`
- `predicate::path::is_file`
- `predicate::path::is_symlink`
- `path_pred = predicate::path::eq_file`
- `path_pred = bytes_pred.from_file_path`- `bytes_pred`.

```
pub enum ContentType {
    Markdown,
    Json,
    Yaml,
    Toml,
    Dockerfile,
    PlainText,
    Unknown,
}
```
## Expand description

# FrontmatterParser in cc_audit::parser::frontmatter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cc-audit/3.14.0/cc_audit/parser/frontmatter/struct.FrontmatterParser.html

`pub struct FrontmatterParser;`## Expand description

Parses YAML frontmatter from markdown files.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Extract frontmatter content from a markdown file.

Frontmatter is delimited by `---` at the start and end.
Returns None if no valid frontmatter is found.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use cc_audit::parser::FrontmatterParser;
let content = "---\nname: test\n---\n# Content";
let frontmatter = FrontmatterParser::extract(content);
assert_eq!(frontmatter, Some("\nname: test\n"));
```

# CveDatabase in cc_audit::cve_db - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cc-audit/3.14.0/cc_audit/cve_db/struct.CveDatabase.html

`pub struct CveDatabase { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

CVE database for querying known vulnerabilities

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cc_audit/cve_db.rs.html#69-295)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-CveDatabase)### impl [CveDatabase](https://docs.rs/struct.CveDatabase.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cc_audit/cve_db.rs.html#69-295)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-CveDatabase)

### impl [CveDatabase](https://docs.rs/struct.CveDatabase.html)

Check if a product/version combination is affected by any CVE Returns matching CVE entries

Check a product/version against all CVEs, ignoring vendor.

An npm package name uniquely identifies a product, but the same package
can be recorded under different vendor strings across databases (the
shipped DB uses `modelcontextprotocol`; a custom DB may use `anthropic`
or `geelen`). Matching on product name avoids brittle vendor coupling
that silently produced zero findings (issue #149).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cc_audit/cve_db.rs.html#255-267)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cc_audit/cve_db.rs.html#255-267)

Create findings for matching CVEs (vendor + product).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cc_audit/cve_db.rs.html#273-284)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cc_audit/cve_db.rs.html#273-284)

Create findings for matching CVEs by product name, ignoring vendor.

Preferred for npm packages, where the package name is the reliable key and the recorded vendor string varies between databases (issue #149).

`pub trait DetectionEngine: `[Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + [Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html) {
    // Required methods
    fn [analyze](https://docs.rs#tymethod.analyze)(
        &self,
        content: &[ParsedContent](https://docs.rs/parser/traits/struct.ParsedContent.html),
        config: &[EngineConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.EngineConfig.html),
    ) -> [AnalysisResult](https://docs.rs/struct.AnalysisResult.html);
[name](https://docs.rs#tymethod.name)(&self) -> &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html);
[can_analyze](https://docs.rs#tymethod.can_analyze)(&self, content: &[ParsedContent](https://docs.rs/parser/traits/struct.ParsedContent.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html);
}## Expand description

Trait for detection engines (L5).

Each engine analyzes parsed content and produces findings. Engines can be composed together for comprehensive analysis.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

    pub min_severity: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Severity](https://docs.rs/rules/types/enum.Severity.html)>,
    pub skip_rules: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>,
    pub context: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>,
}## Expand description

Configuration for the detection engine.

# ContentScanner in cc_audit::engine::scanner - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cc-audit/3.14.0/cc_audit/engine/scanner/trait.ContentScanner.html

`pub trait ContentScanner: `[Scanner](https://docs.rs/trait.Scanner.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [config](https://docs.rs#tymethod.config)(&self) -> &[ScannerConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.ScannerConfig.html);
    // Provided method
    fn [scan_content](https://docs.rs#method.scan_content)(
        &self,
        content: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
        file_path: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),
    ) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Finding](https://docs.rs/rules/types/struct.Finding.html)>> { ... }
}## Expand description

Extended trait for scanners that support content-based scanning.

This trait provides a unified interface for scanning raw content strings, which is useful for testing and for scanners that parse structured files (like JSON) before applying rules.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Scans content and returns findings.

Default implementation delegates to ScannerConfig::check_content. Override this method for scanners that need custom content processing (e.g., JSON parsing, frontmatter extraction).

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

# Confidence in cc_audit::rules::types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cc-audit/3.14.0/cc_audit/rules/types/enum.Confidence.html

# Enum Confidence

[Source](../../../src/cc_audit/rules/types.rs.html#115-123) ```
pub enum Confidence {
    Tentative,
    Firm,
    Certain,
}
```

## Expand description

Confidence level for findings. Higher confidence means less likely to be a false positive.

Tentative: May be a false positive, requires review

Firm: Likely a real issue, but context-dependent

Certain: Very high confidence, unlikely to be a false positive

Downgrade the confidence level by one step.

Used to reduce confidence when heuristics suggest a potential false positive
(e.g., detecting secrets in test files or dummy variable names).

- Certain -> Firm
- Firm -> Tentative
- Tentative -> Tentative (minimum level)

Performs copy-assignment from

`source`.

# RuleSeverity in cc_audit::rules::types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cc-audit/3.14.0/cc_audit/rules/types/enum.RuleSeverity.html

```
pub enum RuleSeverity {
    Warn,
    Error,
}
```
## Expand description

Rule severity level - determines how findings affect CI exit code. This is separate from detection Severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low).

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Warn)

### Warn

Warning: Report only, does not cause CI failure (exit 0)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Error)

### Error

Error: Causes CI failure (exit 1)
